items.prose: A share closes at £100, £120 and then £108 on three days.
items.question: What is the sum of the two daily log returns? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.simple: You added the simple returns, $+20\%$ and $-10\%$. Simple returns do not add; log returns do.
byKey.pct: You gave the simple return over both days, 8%. The log return is $\ln 1.08$.

explain.text: $\ln(120/100) + \ln(108/120) = 0.1823 - 0.1054 = 0.0770 = \ln(108/100)$. The middle price cancels: log returns telescope (lesson 1).

items.prose: Daily noise with mean 5 and sd 2, independent from day to day.
items.question: Is it weakly stationary?

options.text: Yes: its mean, variance and autocovariances do not change over time
No: a stationary series must have mean 0
options.why: You confused a constant mean with a zero mean. Any fixed mean is allowed.

options.text: No: it has no memory
options.why: Memory is not required. White noise is stationary.

options.text: Only after subtracting 5
options.why: Subtracting a constant changes nothing about stationarity; the series is stationary already.

feedback.correct: Correct. Constant is the requirement, not zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the three promises.

explain.text: Mean 5 every day, variance 4 every day, zero covariance at every gap: all three promises hold (lesson 2).

items.prose: An ADF test with a constant on 500 days returns the statistic −3.10. Its critical values are −3.44 (1%), −2.87 (5%) and −2.57 (10%).
items.question: At which levels does it reject a unit root?

options.text: At 5% and 10%, not at 1%
At all three
options.why: −3.10 is not below −3.44, so it does not reach the 1% value.

options.text: At 10% only
options.why: −3.10 is below −2.87 as well, so it rejects at 5% too.

options.text: At none: it is far from −1.645
options.why: You mixed up the direction. Rejection needs the statistic below the critical value, and −3.10 is below two of them.

feedback.correct: Correct. Between the 1% and 5% values: the p-value is between 0.01 and 0.05.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Reject at each level whose critical value the statistic passes on the left.

explain.text: −3.10 lies left of −2.87 and −2.57 but right of −3.44. So $0.01 < p < 0.05$ (lesson 3).

items.prose: A desk fits a share price on its own lag over 2019 to 2021 and gets $p_t = 1.2 + 0.99\,p_{t-1}$.
items.question: Where does its long-horizon forecast settle, in pounds?

feedback.correct: Correct. $1.2/0.01 = 120$: a level learnt from the training years.

byKey.a: You gave the intercept. The forecast settles where $p = a + bp$, at $a/(1 - b)$.
byKey.times: You multiplied the coefficients. Solve $p = 1.2 + 0.99p$ instead.

explain.text: The forecast stops changing where $p = 1.2 + 0.99p$, so $p = 1.2/0.01 = £120$. That level belongs to 2019 to 2021, not to the future (lesson 1).

items.prose: A stationary AR(1) with $\phi = 0.9$ and shock sd $\sigma = 0.5$.
items.question: What is its variance? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.sd: You used $\sigma$ instead of $\sigma^2$ on top.

explain.text: $\gamma_0 = 0.5^2/(1 - 0.9^2) = 0.25/0.19 = 1.3158$: five times the shock variance, because each day carries 90% of yesterday (lesson 2).

items.prose: An analyst differences a series once. The changes have a lag-1 autocorrelation of −0.49 and twice the variance she expected.
items.question: What is the most likely story?

options.text: The series was stationary around a straight trend, and differencing over-differenced it
The series was a random walk, correctly differenced
options.why: A walk's difference is its shocks: no autocorrelation and no extra variance.

options.text: It needs a second difference
options.why: Differencing again would make it worse: the −0.5 correlation is a sign of too many differences, not too few.

options.text: It has a weekly pattern
options.why: A weekly pattern shows at lag 5, not lag 1.

feedback.correct: Correct. $\varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}$ gives a correlation of −0.5 and a variance of $2\sigma^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does differencing do to noise around a line?

explain.text: Noise around a line, differenced, becomes $b + \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}$: lag-1 correlation −0.5 and variance $2\sigma^2$. The fix is to detrend instead (lesson 4).

items.prose: In seeded simulations of an AR(1) with $\phi = 0.98$, the 5% Dickey-Fuller test rejected 12% of 2,000 paths of 250 days. It rejected 85% of 1,000 paths of 1,000 days.
items.question: A spread with 250 days of history gives ADF p = 0.40. What should you say?

options.text: Not rejecting is weak evidence: even a reverting spread would usually give this result with 250 days
The spread has a unit root
options.why: You read non-rejection as proof. At $\phi = 0.98$ the test misses 88% of the time.

options.text: There is a 40% chance it has a unit root
options.why: A p-value is not the probability of the null.

options.text: Use the normal critical value for more power
options.why: That would reject true walks nearly half the time: power bought with false alarms.

feedback.correct: Correct. Low power makes non-rejection uninformative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the power numbers in the prose.

explain.text: The test finds $\phi = 0.98$ only 12% of the time with 250 days. So p = 0.40 is the expected result even if the spread reverts. Four times the data raises power to 85% (lesson 3).

items.prose: Two seeded series, each 500 days: lesson 4's walk and its straight trend plus noise. ADF p-values with a constant ("c") and with a constant and trend ("ct"):
items.question: Which series should be detrended rather than differenced?

options.text: B: it rejects a unit root once the trend term is in
A: it fails both tests
options.why: Failing both means a stochastic trend, which needs differencing.

options.text: Both
options.why: A keeps its unit root even with a trend term; detrending would leave it wandering.

options.text: Neither: difference both
options.why: Differencing B, which is stationary around a line, over-differences it.

feedback.correct: Correct. B is trend-stationary; A has a unit root.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the "ct" column.

explain.text: B rejects with "ct" (p < 0.0001): stationary around a line, so detrend it. A fails both (0.52 and 0.77): a stochastic trend, so difference it (lesson 4).
